title: GOD KNEW WE WOULD BREAK HIS HEART… SO WHY DOES GENESIS SAY HE REGRETTED MAKING US?
paragraphs: GOD KNEW WE WOULD BREAK HIS HEART… SO WHY DOES GENESIS SAY HE REGRETTED MAKING US?
The terrifying truth behind Genesis 6:6, the Hebrew word that changes how we understand God's grief, and the breathtaking grace of a Savior who knew our worst before choosing the cross.
What if I told you that one of the most heartbreaking sentences in the entire Bible is not spoken by a suffering human being…
But written about God Himself?
Not when Adam hid among the trees.
Not when Cain murdered his brother.
Not even when Judas betrayed Jesus with a kiss.
It happened when God looked upon the humanity He had created, saw what had become of the hearts He had given life to, and Scripture recorded something almost unbearable:
“And it repented the LORD that he had made man on the earth, and it grieved him at his heart.” — Genesis 6:6 (KJV)
Read that again.
The Creator of the universe was grieved at His heart.
The One who spoke galaxies into existence looked upon His own creation, and what He saw brought divine sorrow.
But here is the question that has troubled thoughtful believers for centuries.
If God already knew humanity would become wicked, why does the Bible say He regretted making us?
Did God make a mistake?
Did humanity surprise Him?
Did the all-knowing Creator discover something He had not anticipated?
And if God could regret creating humanity, could He someday regret saving you?
That last question is where this becomes painfully personal.
Because perhaps you have never asked whether God regretted creating humanity.
But somewhere in the silence after another failure, another secret sin, another promise you broke, you may have wondered…
“Does God regret making me?”
Stay with that question.
Because the answer takes us from the corruption before Noah's flood to the bloodstained cross of Jesus Christ.
And what we discover may change the way you understand both God's holiness and His love.
Genesis 6 does not begin with a God who has suddenly lost control.
It begins with a humanity that has become horrifyingly comfortable with evil.
Scripture declares:
“And GOD saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually.” — Genesis 6:5 (KJV)
Notice the language.
Not merely that people occasionally committed wicked acts.
Not merely that society had developed some unfortunate habits.
The corruption had penetrated the imagination, the thoughts, and the intentions of the human heart.
Evil was no longer simply something people did.
It had become something they continually cultivated.
And the Hebrew text makes the diagnosis even more disturbing.
The phrase describing the human heart includes the words:
כָּל־יֵצֶר מַחְשְׁבֹת לִבּוֹ
Kol-yetser machshevot libbo.
A close rendering is “every inclination of the thoughts of his heart.”
The Hebrew word יֵצֶר (yetser) refers to an inclination, formation, or intention. Here it concerns the inward disposition of human thinking.
The issue was not simply outward misconduct.
It was the direction of the inner life.
And that is uncomfortable because we are often much better at managing appearances than confronting motives.
We know how to look faithful while hiding resentment.
How to speak about forgiveness while secretly rehearsing revenge.
How to raise our hands in worship while refusing to surrender the very sin the Holy Spirit has been exposing.
How to post a Bible verse while privately feeding something that is slowly destroying us.
We know how to convince other people that everything is fine.
Sometimes we even convince ourselves.
But Genesis 6 reminds us of something we desperately need to remember:
God sees what the world applauds, what the world ignores, and what we desperately try to conceal.
He sees the public behavior.
And He sees the private heart.
That is why the next verse is so devastating.
“And it repented the LORD that he had made man on the earth, and it grieved him at his heart.” — Genesis 6:6 (KJV)
Now we arrive at the word that creates the controversy.
Regretted.
Repented.
Was sorry.
Different English translations express the verse differently, and that difference matters.
The Hebrew verb is:
וַיִּנָּחֶם — vayyinnāḥem
It comes from the Hebrew root נחם (n-ḥ-m), a word that can communicate sorrow, regret, relenting, or consolation, depending on its grammatical form and context.
In Genesis 6:6, the verb conveys divine regret or sorrow concerning humanity's creation in light of humanity's wickedness.
But there is something we must understand before we build an entire theology around one English word.
The Bible does not use the word “regret” in every context to mean that someone made an ignorant mistake.
Human regret often involves discovering information we did not possess.
We say, “If only I had known.”
We regret a decision because we could not see its consequences.
But Scripture does not present God as a limited creature learning history as it unfolds.
Isaiah 46:10 speaks of God declaring the end from the beginning.
Psalm 139:4 describes His knowledge of our words before they are spoken.

And Acts 2:23 teaches that the crucifixion of Jesus occurred according to God's definite plan and foreknowledge, even while those responsible for crucifying Him remained accountable for their wicked actions.
God's foreknowledge is not an afterthought.
It is part of how Scripture reveals His sovereignty.
So when Genesis says God regretted making humanity, it does not require us to believe that God suddenly discovered human evil or wished He could travel backward to correct an unforeseen mistake.
Instead, the passage reveals God's genuine moral response to the evil that had overtaken His creation.
The same God who knew what humanity would do truly opposed what humanity had become.
Knowing that evil will occur does not mean approving of evil when it occurs.
Think about that.
A parent may know that a child is moving toward a destructive decision.
The warning signs may be unmistakable.
The consequences may be predictable.
Yet when that child finally walks into destruction, the parent's sorrow is not imaginary.
Foreknowledge does not make heartbreak meaningless.
That human analogy is limited, of course. God is not merely a more informed human parent.
But it helps expose the mistaken assumption behind the question.
We assume that if someone knew something beforehand, they cannot genuinely grieve when it happens.
Scripture does not make that assumption.
And Genesis goes even further.
The second expression in verse 6 says:
וַיִּתְעַצֵּב אֶל־לִבּוֹ
Vayyit'atsev el-libbo.
A close translation is “and He was grieved to His heart.”
The Hebrew verb comes from עצב (ʿ-ts-b), associated here with grief or pain.
The language is profoundly personal.
Genesis is not describing a cold administrator disappointed that His project failed to meet expectations.
It portrays the living God responding to human corruption with grief.
This is language that communicates God's relationship to His creation in terms human beings can understand.
Theologians often describe such expressions as anthropopathic language—language that speaks of God using human emotional categories.
But that does not mean the passage is empty poetry or that God's opposition to evil is pretend.
It means Scripture is communicating something true about God without requiring us to imagine Him as an ignorant, unstable, or helpless human being.
God's grief is real. His knowledge is not defective. His holiness is not negotiable.
And then comes the apparent contradiction.
Numbers 23:19 declares:
“God is not a man, that he should lie; neither the son of man, that he should repent: hath he said, and shall he not do it? or hath he spoken, and shall he not make it good?” (KJV)
Wait.
Genesis says God regretted.
Numbers says God does not repent.
Both passages use forms of the same Hebrew root, n-ḥ-m.
So which one is true?
Both.
But only when we stop forcing two different passages to answer exactly the same question.
Numbers 23 takes place in the account of Balaam and Balak.
Balak wanted Israel cursed.
But God had determined to bless His people, and Balaam could not overturn that divine purpose.
Numbers 23:19 emphasizes that God is not like a deceitful or unreliable human being who lies, reverses His promises capriciously, or fails to accomplish what He has spoken.
The immediate context makes that meaning clear.
God is faithful to His declared word.
He is not manipulated by human pressure.
He does not change His promises because someone offers Him a better deal.
Genesis 6, however, is addressing something different.
It describes God's grief over pervasive human wickedness and His decision to bring judgment upon a corrupt world.
One passage reveals the seriousness of God's moral response to sin.
The other reveals the dependability of God's word.
They are not competing descriptions of a confused deity.
They are complementary revelations of the same holy God.
And there is another passage that makes this distinction especially clear.
In 1 Samuel 15:11, God declares that He regrets having made Saul king.
Yet in the same chapter, verse 29 says that the Glory of Israel does not lie or have regret like a man.
The biblical writer places these statements in the same narrative.
That should caution us against assuming that every use of the word “regret” means exactly the same thing.
God can express grief over human rebellion and announce a change in His dealings with people without becoming dishonest, ignorant, or unfaithful.
Jeremiah 18:7–10 also explains that God's announced dealings with nations can respond to repentance or continued evil.
When people turn from wickedness, He may relent from announced disaster.
When people abandon righteousness, He may withhold announced blessing.
This is not divine inconsistency.
It is consistent moral government.
God's holiness does not change when His dealings with human beings change.
His faithfulness does not disappear when He judges rebellion.
And His mercy does not contradict His justice when He forgives the repentant.
Here is where the story becomes more frightening.
Because if Genesis 6 teaches us anything, it is that God's patience must never be mistaken for indifference.
The world before the flood continued living.
People had ordinary routines.
They made plans.
They built lives.
They likely imagined tomorrow would resemble yesterday.
But beneath the apparent normalcy was a civilization whose wickedness had become intolerable.
Genesis 6:11 describes the earth as corrupt and filled with violence.
God saw it.
And God did not call evil good simply because evil had become common.
That should disturb us.
Not because we can identify exactly when modern society has reached the condition described in Noah's generation.
Scripture does not authorize us to make that calculation.
But because the same moral warning confronts every generation.
A culture can normalize what God condemns.
A crowd can celebrate what Scripture calls destructive.
And a person can become so accustomed to sin that conviction begins to feel like an inconvenience rather than a mercy.
There is a terrifying kind of spiritual blindness in which we no longer ask whether something pleases God.
We only ask whether we can get away with it.
And sometimes the most dangerous moment in a person's spiritual life is not when they feel guilty.
It is when they stop feeling troubled at all.
Yet even here, in one of the darkest chapters of Genesis, a remarkable sentence interrupts the judgment.
“But Noah found grace in the eyes of the LORD.” — Genesis 6:8 (KJV)
But Noah.
Two words that change the atmosphere of the story.
The world was corrupt.
Violence was widespread.
Judgment was approaching.
But Noah found grace.
The Hebrew says:
וְנֹחַ מָצָא חֵן בְּעֵינֵי יְהוָה
Ve-Noach matza chen be'einei YHWH.
A close rendering is “But Noah found favor in the eyes of the LORD.”
The word חֵן (chen) means favor or grace.
Notice what appears in the story before the ark is constructed.
Grace.
Before the rain.
Before the waters rose.
Before the door was shut.
There was grace.
Noah's story is not permission to imagine that he earned salvation through flawless moral performance.
Genesis 6:9 describes him as righteous and blameless among his contemporaries, and as one who walked with God.
Hebrews 11:7 connects Noah's righteousness with faith.
The Bible presents Noah as a man who trusted God and responded in obedience.
The ark did not make Noah worthy of God's favor.
It became the appointed means through which God preserved Noah and his household.
And that points us toward something far greater.
Because Noah's story does not end with humanity permanently cured of sin.
After the flood, Genesis 8:21 still speaks of the evil inclination of the human heart.
The waters removed a wicked generation.
They did not remove the deeper problem of human sinfulness.
Humanity needed more than a fresh environment.
More than a second chance.
More than another warning.
We needed redemption.
And that is where the story moves toward Jesus.
The New Testament explicitly connects Noah's flood with Christian salvation.
First Peter 3:20–21 recalls those saved through water in Noah's day and speaks of baptism in relation to salvation through the resurrection of Jesus Christ.

Peter does not teach that water possesses magical power to wash away sin. He explicitly distinguishes the matter from merely removing dirt from the body and directs attention to the resurrection of Christ.
The point is that deliverance from judgment finds its ultimate Christian meaning in Jesus.
And suddenly, the question we began with becomes even more astonishing.
Why did God create humanity knowing that humanity would rebel?
Scripture does not reveal every detail of God's eternal purposes, and we should not pretend to possess explanations He has not given.
But it does reveal something extraordinary.
God's plan of redemption was not an emergency response to an unexpected human disaster.
First Peter 1:19–20 describes Christ as a lamb without blemish or spot, foreknown before the foundation of the world and manifested in the last times for our sake.
Ephesians 1:4–7 speaks of God's gracious purpose in Christ, including redemption through His blood and the forgiveness of sins.
The cross was not God's desperate attempt to rescue a creation that had slipped beyond His foresight.
The saving work of Jesus belongs to God's eternal redemptive purpose.
And now consider what that means.
Before Judas sold Him out, Jesus knew betrayal would come.
Before Peter denied Him, Jesus knew the rooster would crow.
Before the soldiers drove nails through His hands, the suffering of Christ was already within God's saving purpose.
Before the crowd demanded crucifixion, Jesus had come to give His life as a ransom for many.
He was not caught off guard by human wickedness.
He came to confront it, bear sin's judgment, and accomplish redemption.
And this is where the Gospel becomes almost too beautiful to comprehend.
The God who grieved over humanity's wickedness is the God who gave His Son to save sinners.
John 3:16 does not say God loved the world because the world had finally become lovable.
It says:
“For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son…” (KJV)
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (KJV)
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we had repaired our reputations.
Not after we had defeated every temptation.
Not after we had made ourselves impressive enough to deserve attention.
While we were still sinners.
That does not make sin insignificant.
It makes grace astonishing.
Because the cross is not God pretending our rebellion never mattered.
The cross reveals just how seriously God takes sin and how far His mercy reaches to redeem those who trust in Christ.
Jesus did not die so we could remain comfortably enslaved to the very evil that required His sacrifice.
He died and rose again so that sinners could be forgiven, reconciled to God, and transformed by His grace.
That is why repentance matters.
Repentance is not a performance designed to purchase God's affection.
It is a genuine turning from sin toward God.
It is the surrender of our excuses.
The abandonment of our cherished rebellion.
The willingness to stop defending what Christ came to save us from.
And perhaps that is what you need to hear today.
Not another message telling you that your mistakes do not matter.
They do matter.
Sin destroys.
Sin deceives.
Sin wounds people who never deserved to be wounded.
Sin hardens hearts and fractures relationships.
And no amount of religious vocabulary can turn darkness into light.
But your sin is not greater than the saving power of Jesus Christ.
Your past is not beyond His knowledge.
Your failures did not catch Him by surprise.
And the person you have become does not have to be the person you remain.
Maybe you are reading this after returning to a habit you promised God you would abandon.
Maybe you have been smiling in church while your marriage is collapsing at home.
Maybe you have spent years trying to appear spiritually strong because you are terrified that someone will discover how exhausted you really are.
Maybe your family knows a version of you that your church never sees.
Or maybe you have been away from God so long that even the thought of praying feels dishonest.
You know the words.
You remember the songs.
You can still quote the verses.
But deep inside, you are wondering whether you have exhausted God's patience.
Hear what Scripture actually says.
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” — John 6:37 (KJV)
Those are the words of Jesus.
Not a promise that repentance is unnecessary.
Not permission to embrace sin without consequence.
But a breathtaking assurance that those who truly come to Christ are not rejected by Him.
And 1 John 1:9 declares:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (KJV)
Faithful.
Just.
Forgive.
Cleanse.
Those are not the words of a Savior who is powerless to restore.
They are the words of a Gospel that can reach into the places where shame has convinced you that hope is dead.
So return to the question that started everything.
Does God regret making you?
Genesis 6 does not give us permission to declare God's private feelings about any particular individual.
It is a passage about humanity's corruption, divine grief, and righteous judgment.
But the Gospel does give us a clear answer to the fear beneath that question.
God is not ignorant of your sin.
He is not indifferent to it.
And He has not left repentant sinners without a Savior.
Jesus Christ came into the world to save sinners (1 Timothy 1:15).
He lived without sin.
He died for our sins according to the Scriptures.
He was buried.
And He rose again on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
The invitation is not to deny your guilt.
It is to bring your guilt to the One who can forgive it.
Not to pretend your heart is clean.
But to come to the One who can make you new.
This is why the Gospel Warrior message will always return to one truth:
Not because Jesus changes the historical facts of your past.
He does not make yesterday's betrayal something that never happened.
He does not erase the real consequences that others may still carry.
But He can forgive sin, change the sinner, teach us to make amends where possible, and write a redeemed future that our past could never have produced on its own.
The scandal is real.
The guilt is real.
The judgment of God is real.
But so is the grace of Jesus Christ.
And that grace is not cheap.
It was purchased through the suffering and death of the Son of God.
If this truth has exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to write your private sins publicly for strangers to examine.
But you can take a small, honest step toward surrender.
There are battles that become heavier when we insist on fighting them alone.
You may discover that someone reading your words has been carrying a similar struggle in silence.
That is one reason this message matters beyond the person currently reading it.
Somewhere on your Facebook friends list is someone who still believes their worst mistake has disqualified them from God's mercy.
Someone who has stopped praying.
Someone who feels too ashamed to walk back into church.
Someone who has confused God's holiness with the idea that forgiveness is impossible.
Not merely because you agree with it.
But because someone who would never search for a sermon may encounter the Gospel through something you share.
There may come a night when the old questions return.
When shame whispers that God could never welcome someone like you.
When the enemy of your soul tries to convince you that your failures are more powerful than Christ's finished work.
Come back to these Scriptures.
Read them again.
Not to manufacture an emotional feeling.
But to remember what God has actually said.

We want this community to be a place where difficult questions are not buried beneath shallow answers, where Scripture is examined carefully, where sin is confronted truthfully, and where the grace of Jesus Christ is proclaimed without compromise.
Not as a payment for God's favor.
Not as a requirement for salvation.
But if Gospel Warrior has helped you understand Scripture, return to prayer, confront sin, or grow closer to Jesus, you have an opportunity to help this ministry continue and expand.
Yet Scripture does affirm the value of freely supporting Gospel ministry.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
“God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
And 3 John 1:8 encourages believers to support those who labor for the truth so that they may become fellow helpers in that work.
That is the spirit of this invitation.
Not pressure.
Partnership.
Those free resources remain an important part of our mission.
Because the goal is not to place biblical nourishment behind a financial wall.
The goal is to make more of it available.
Your prayers matter.
Your willingness to share sound biblical teaching matters.
Your decision to encourage another struggling believer matters.
Your commitment to follow Jesus matters far more than any financial contribution.
We are all dependent on the same grace.
And that brings us back, one final time, to Genesis 6.
Imagine Noah hearing the warnings of God.
Imagine the weight of building an ark while the world around him continued in corruption.
Imagine the seriousness of knowing that judgment was coming.
And then imagine the mercy of being preserved through that judgment.
Now look toward Calvary.
Not at a wooden ark, but at a wooden cross.
Not at Noah, a faithful but imperfect man.
But at Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God.
The One who bore our sins.
The One who rose from the dead.
The One who calls sinners to repent and believe the Gospel.
Genesis 6 teaches us that God does not take human wickedness lightly.
Numbers 23 teaches us that God does not lie or abandon His faithful word.
And the cross reveals that God's holiness and saving love are not enemies.
They meet in the redemptive work of Jesus Christ.
So perhaps the question that should keep us awake tonight is no longer simply:
“Why did God regret making humanity if He already knew what humans would do?”
Perhaps the deeper question is this:
“If God knew the full extent of human rebellion, why did He still choose to reveal such extraordinary mercy through His Son?”
We cannot explain every mystery of God's eternal counsel.
But we can stand before the cross and know this:
His love was not born from ignorance.
His grace was not an accident.
And His promise of salvation in Christ is not a fragile hope that disappears when we finally recognize how sinful we have been.
The God who sees the hidden heart calls us out of hiding.
The God who judges evil commands us to repent.
And the God who gave His Son offers forgiveness and new life to everyone who turns to Jesus Christ in faith.
So do not leave this article merely fascinated by an ancient Hebrew word.
Let the Word of God search your heart.
Let it expose what needs repentance.
Let it strengthen what has become weak.
Let it bring you back to the Savior.
And if you have never truly surrendered your life to Jesus Christ, you can begin by turning to Him now, confessing your sin, and trusting in His death and resurrection rather than your own goodness.
Because the greatest tragedy would not be discovering that God grieved over humanity's wickedness.
It would be hearing about the grace offered in Jesus Christ and choosing to remain in the darkness.
God knew how far humanity would fall. Yet in Christ, He revealed how far His mercy would reach to save.
